cards.explanation: The answer is light, friends. The Teacher says "…wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). He looks at both and says wisdom wins. It's plain as turning on the kitchen light and seeing where the cookie sheet actually is.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher first says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness. Then comes the turn: "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). Same fate for both, and that's what rattles him.

The answer is that he asks what being wise gained him, friends. He says to himself, "The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). He's looking at all that wisdom and wondering what it bought him. I think that question sat heavy with him.

The answer is forgotten, friends. The Teacher says "…there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Wise or foolish, the remembering fades for both. Every wise man and every fool, same boat.
The answer is that he hated life, friends. The Teacher says plainly, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). That's a heavy thing to say. I think he really means it.

The answer is that the work people do was painful to him, friends. He says, "…I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The work itself weighed on him. Then he sums it up: "…everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind."

The answer is that he must leave it to the man after him, friends. He says, "I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). All that work, and it goes to someone else. I think that stings.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher says, "…my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Despair, not peace. A few verses later he says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24).

The answer is evil, friends. When a man who labored with wisdom, knowledge and skill must give his portion to one who hasn't worked for it, the Teacher says "…this too is futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). Those are his exact words. I think that one stings.
The answer is mind, friends. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Night comes and the thoughts keep right on going. That's one busy mind.

The answer is to eat and drink and enjoy his work, friends. That's the turn. After all that heaviness, the Teacher says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Simple things, taken as they come. I think the room gets a little lighter right here.

The answer is True, friends. The Teacher says, "I have also seen that this is from the hand of God." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Eating, drinking and enjoying your work are not something you squeeze out alone. They come from God's hand.

The answer is gathering what he'll hand to one who pleases God, friends. The text says, "…to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The sinner gathers, and the one who pleases God receives it. The verse closes by calling this "…futile and a pursuit of the wind."
